items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: Jim O’Heir and Zachary Levi Are Starring in a New Comedy About a Pastor Working the Grocery Store Checkout
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Shelf Life, a new comedy from the producers of The Promised Land, follows a pastor who loses his pulpit and ends up working at a grocery store. Jim O’Heir (Parks and Recreation) and Zachary Levi (Shazam!) lead the cast, and the series is set to premiere exclusively on the Angel platform in 2027. She
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Shelf Life, a new comedy from the producers of The Promised Land, follows a pastor who loses his pulpit and ends up working at a grocery store. Jim O’Heir (Parks and Recreation) and Zachary Levi (Shazam!) lead the cast, and the series is set to premiere exclusively on the Angel platform in 2027.

Shelf Life is created, written and directed by Brian Cates and produced by Milk & Honey Studios. It is currently in production. The premise is a former pastor who is kicked out of the pulpit takes a job at a local grocery store, where he realizes his calling to care for others can’t be shelved while surrounded by quirky coworkers. The cast also includes Wesam Keesh, Donna Biscoe, Tommy Woodard, Jonathan Charles, Leilany Celeste, Jazelle Villanueva and Brittany Visser. Richie Johns produces.

Mitch Hudson, an executive producer on the series, shared the news on Instagram. “It’s official – I’m executive producing a comedy series starring Jim O’Heir and Zachary Levi!” he wrote. He said Cates has “an incredible vision” as creator and director, that his business partner Johns is leading the producing team, and that Milk & Honey Studios is adding “another comedy show to our lineup” with Angel as a partner. “More info coming soon!” he added.

Cates said he has spent 20 years working in the faith and comedy space and believes “if you make people laugh, you can make people listen.” He described the show as something families can watch together, “genuinely funny, but also honest about life, faith, failure and second chances.” The message, he said, is that “we all reach moments when we think we’ve passed our expiration date. But God isn’t finished with us yet.”

O’Heir said that with Shelf Life “you come for the laughs, but you end up genuinely caring about these people.”

items.title: Bl. Fulton Sheen’s Hidden Interior Life
items.author: Nell O’Leary
items.summary:
Nell O’Leary

Like Sheen, if we allow Christ to reveal himself to us, to transform us through the graces he alone offers, then we can live in the overflow of those graces to proclaim him in the culture.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Nell O’Leary

In September, Archbishop Fulton J. Sheen was beatified: the premier evangelist of the twentieth century; an Emmy Award winner; friend to European royalty and Hollywood stars alike; a farmer’s son sent from Peoria to study at the Saint Paul Seminary, Catholic University of America, and Louvain, who went on to earn multiple honors and advanced degrees; a man with a sensitive stomach who slept little and worked exhaustively; and an ardent adorer of the Blessed Sacrament who died during his daily morning holy hour after sixty-one years of the devotional practice. And in all this, he was beatified neither because of his fame nor his evangelistic reach but rather because of his radical intimacy with God. 

The remarkable beatification was a national event gathering over fifty thousand people in St. Louis, Missouri: bishops, priests, deacons, seminarians, religious brothers and sisters, old people, babies, and every person in between. Culturally, we would associate a celebration the size of Sheen’s beatification with being proportionate to his own fame and reach. Famous guy = big party. As Catholics and Christians, we see something different. Holy guy = big party. People came with memories of watching him on television and hearing him on the radio; some even had known him personally. Internationally known bishops, nationally famous podcasters, actors, musicians, artists, all prayed alongside the most ordinary of all ordinary lay persons in the pew. It was exactly the mix of folks Sheen would have loved to see. 

The process for beatification involves many years of interviewing people to prove that the candidate lived a life of heroic virtue. Those conversations are compiled into a large tome called a positio. Simultaneously, investigations are undertaken into alleged miracles attributed to the candidate’s intercessory prayer. Sheen was found to not only intercede for a baby, James Fulton Engstrom—who went sixty-one minutes (the same number of years of his holy hour practice) without a heartbeat and now is a healthy, wonderful teenage young man—but he also lived a life according to the virtues. As then-Fr. Robert Barron wrote about the beatification of Pope John Paul II, “And what exactly is virtue? The Church has identified the ‘cardinal’ virtues of justice, temperance, prudence and fortitude and the ‘theological’ virtues of faith, hope and love. . . . [A saint is] someone who has remarkably embodied these moral and spiritual excellences.” Sheen embodied these excellences, and the Church was delighted to celebrate this remarkable man. 

I was privileged to be present for the events leading up to the beatification and the beatification Mass. I saw the crowds of folks shuffling through the expo hall. I heard the roar of the audience at the morning’s entertainment event. I witnessed the forty-five-minute procession at Mass of over one thousand men: cardinals, bishops, priests, deacons, and seminarians. I sang along with the magnificent choir and orchestra during Mass. I wept when my old friends, the Engstrom family, whose son’s healing was the miracle cause for the beatification, processed up with Sheen’s jawbone relic. The Sheen Foundation certainly put incredible time and effort into each detail of the remarkable gathering to hear the pronouncement of beatification from Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the papal delegate. 

But as I heard it, something moved in my heart beyond the crowds and the clamor, the commotion and the clapping. Sheen shows us all the exterior aspects are important, but at the end of the day, it’s the interior that really counts. 

Sheen led a remarkably public life: teaching at CUA for nearly twenty-five years; speaking on his radio show The Catholic Hour, which reached four million households over twenty years; filming his television show Life Is Worth Living for nearly a decade, reaching up to ten million viewers a week; writing nearly seventy books on a variety of topics; and serving as national director for the Propagation for the Faith for nearly fifteen years, raising millions for the missions around the world. He led an even more remarkable private life, one we know of from interviews, letters, and stories told posthumously. It was this proof of heroic virtue that brought him to beatification, not the tens of thousands of conversions, high- and low-profile, not the personal relationships with popes, or the speaking tours around the world. The hidden life—one of interior union with God—is what we are actually called to emulate. 

Word on Fire has a particular tagline: Proclaim Christ in the culture. Not “to” the culture. Not “at” the culture. Not “towards” the culture. The choice of that preposition holds great meaning. I would venture a guess to say that one can only proclaim something “in”—a position of relationship. If I’m “in” the room, I can speak to people inside of it. If I’m near or outside of or adjacent to, my reach is limited by proximity and access. Fulton Sheen lived this out in a very specific way. He entered whole-heartedly into relationship with everyone he encountered. He brought Christ into the conversation, the exchanges of humor, the moments of carrying the suffering of the other. He stepped in. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

If we look at the wide-ranging biographies of saints and venerables, those who lived with a deep desire to be intimately close with the Lord, they include this profundity in common. Some led public ministry—many did not. Sheen lived his successful outreach from a simple place of deep interior intimacy with our Lord Jesus. He credits his practice of a daily holy hour that he began at seminary for the graces necessary to do the work that the Lord offered to him. He offered himself to God and found that he could then live in the overflow of those graces and that intimacy. That overflow is where we see that, time and again, he touched the lives of others by stepping outside of himself and into their story, whether it was a cold and hungry man on the curb or a woman in the elevator of a hospital visiting a dying parent or the flight attendant with a wounded past. He saw them as God’s beloved children and entered into their stories. 

I’m not saying that our takeaway from Sheen’s example is to remain purposely hidden, and I am also not saying it is to order a ring light and whip up a fee-based video platform so as to evangelize. Upon examining his life, his writing, and his impact, Sheen believed that God’s desire is for us, fully and intimately. If we podcast, great. If we listen to our neighbor’s woes and pray with them, greater. If we allow Christ to reveal himself to us, to transform us through the graces he alone offers, then we can live in the overflow of those graces to proclaim him in the culture. Sheen may be the world’s most famous evangelist, but he’s recognized as a blessed because in the small, hidden rhythms of his day, he chose to habituate virtue, cooperate with grace, and be obediently intimate with the workings of the Holy Spirit. You and I are called the same. Let’s begin today. Nunc coepi.
